grammar[0].fact: German word parts add up: *Schlaf*, *schlafen*, *schläfrig*, *einschlafen*, *ausschlafen*, *verschlafen* (to oversleep), *Schlaflosigkeit*. Learn one family, and you get a dozen words for the price of a single root.

grammar[1].blocks[1].note: When the two cases differ, the der-word is needed.
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: The preposition goes in front
grammar[1].blocks[2].note: English leaves it at the end (the town I grew up in); German never does.
grammar[1].blocks[3].title: Words for the practice page
grammar[1].fact: Many old German proverbs begin this way: *Wer rastet, der rostet*, who rests, rusts. *Wer A sagt, muss auch B sagen*: who says A has to say B. *Wer zuletzt lacht, lacht am besten*. A proverb is a useful way to remember the grammar.

document.intro: A real sign on a tree at the edge of a German wood. It’s a request, and it’s stern. *Wildtiere* are wild animals, and *Hunde sind an der Leine zu führen* is the *ist zu* form: dogs must be on a lead.
document.fact: Three exclamation marks on a German sign mean somebody has been upset. *Der Eigentümer*, signed at the bottom, is the owner, and in Germany you may walk in almost any wood, by law, even if it’s private. So he can only ask.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Say each rule with wer: Wer …, muss …
reading.intro: Max sleeps badly. His doctor has sent him to a sleep lab in Cologne for one night. There are eleven wires on his head, and a camera on the ceiling. The night nurse has given him a form. Then Dr. Berg, who’s in charge, comes on the speaker at midnight.
reading.fact: And there’s the German *Bettdecke*: couples often have two separate duvets, each neatly folded on a split mattress. Foreign guests are often surprised by this.
